paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately support vector regression can recover a linear relationship from noisy measurements. It considers both hard and soft versions, asking when the hard formulation has a valid solution and how well either version predicts new data. The analysis focuses on high-dimensional settings under assumptions about the statistical distribution of the data.

For hard support vector regression, the authors characterize feasibility and derive an asymptotic approximation to prediction risk when a solution exists. For the soft version, they describe how test risk depends on the algorithm’s parameters. These results turn parameter selection into a problem informed by predicted performance rather than treating the settings as fixed.

A central finding is that adding training examples can hurt test performance when parameters are not appropriately chosen. Within the analyzed setting, optimally selecting those parameters makes additional samples beneficial. The implication is that the relationship between dataset size and accuracy depends on tuning: more data and unchanged settings need not produce the same trend as more data with optimal settings.
icml-2021-a-precise-performance-analysis.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis of support vector regression explains its prediction risk and why optimal tuning matters when adding data.

paragraphs: Evaluating a neural network or generating samples with an autoregressive model often requires computations to happen in a strict sequence. That dependency limits how much extra computing hardware can help. This paper reformulates feedforward computation as a system of nonlinear equations, creating another route to the same outputs.

The authors solve those equations using Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel fixed-point iterations, together with methods that combine them. Jacobi updates are especially useful because each equation can be updated independently, allowing simultaneous execution. The approach guarantees the same values as the original computation using no more parallelizable iterations, with fewer iterations possible. A reduction in elapsed time depends on having sufficient parallel computing power.

Experiments apply the approach to recurrent-network backpropagation, DenseNet evaluation, and autoregressive sampling with MADE and PixelCNN++. Reported speedups range from 2.1 to 26 across the tested settings. The contribution is a way to reorganize computation while preserving its result, showing that apparently sequential machine-learning workloads can sometimes benefit substantially from parallel equation solving.
icml-2021-accelerating-feedforward-compu.tldr: Recasting feedforward computation as nonlinear equation solving enables parallel execution with identical outputs and substantial reported speedups.

paragraphs: The examples presented during training, and how their sampling changes over time, influence how a deep-learning model learns. Choosing an entire sampling schedule is difficult because it contains many decisions, making it a high-dimensional hyperparameter. AutoSampling addresses this problem by automatically searching for schedules that support effective model training.

The method combines two kinds of search. A multi-exploitation step looks for effective local schedules, using shortened exploitation cycles to obtain enough feedback for the search. An exploration step periodically estimates a sampling distribution from the schedules already learned and then perturbs that distribution. This lets the method investigate changes in the broader sampling distribution as well as adjustments to local schedules.

The authors argue that combining these searches produces a robust sampling schedule and demonstrate the method on several image-classification tasks. The significance is that data sampling becomes something the training process can learn, with local feedback informing broader exploration. The stated evidence concerns the effectiveness of this combined approach on the classification tasks examined.
icml-2021-autosampling-search-for-effect.tldr: AutoSampling learns training-data sampling schedules by combining local schedule search with exploration of sampling distributions.

paragraphs: An agent can learn about its environment by performing actions that reveal how the world behaves. This paper develops that idea through causal curiosity, an intrinsic reward that encourages reinforcement-learning agents to discover useful experiments. The aim is to categorize resulting trajectories and infer causal factors in a hierarchy.

The learned action sequences expose differences in environmental dynamics and support binary, quantized representations of the underlying causal factors. The experiments can have recognizable meanings: to distinguish heavy blocks from light ones, agents learn to lift them. The authors report that these behaviors emerge through self-supervision using approximately 2.5 times less data than conventional supervised planners.

The paper also studies what these experiments enable beyond the original discovery task. Learned behaviors can be reused and fine-tuned, including transferring from lifting to pushing or other downstream activities. Knowledge of the causal representations also helps zero-shot learning on more complex tasks. Together, the findings connect active experimentation, learned representations, and subsequent task learning in the environments studied.
icml-2021-causal-curiosity-rl-agents-dis.tldr: Causal curiosity rewards agents for discovering informative experiments that reveal causal factors and support later task learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization helps choose evaluations of an expensive black-box function. Several parties could search the same function together, sharing the work of finding good inputs. But when evaluated outcomes correspond to rewards such as money, an efficient collective search can still be unattractive if some participants receive substantially worse outcomes than others.

This paper introduces a notion of regret that incorporates both efficiency and fairness, drawing on social-welfare ideas from economics. Regret represents the cost of making less successful choices during optimization. The authors develop a collaborative algorithm alongside this measure, with an adjustable parameter in both that controls the tradeoff between collective efficiency and fairness among participants.

The analysis bounds the new regret to provide a theoretical convergence-rate guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate benefits including increased fairness. The contribution is therefore both an evaluation criterion and an optimization procedure: it makes the distribution of search outcomes among collaborators part of the objective, rather than assessing collaboration solely through aggregate inefficiency.
icml-2021-collaborative-bayesian-optimiz.tldr: A collaborative Bayesian optimization method explicitly trades off overall search efficiency against fairness in participants’ accumulated rewards.

paragraphs: Contrastive representation learning often tries to capture information shared by different views of the same underlying content. These views might be augmented versions of an image or different portions of a sequence. The paper addresses a weakness of common contrastive objectives: their lower bounds can substantially underestimate mutual information when the views share a large amount.

Decomposed Estimation of Mutual Information, or DEMI, divides this large estimation problem into smaller pieces. One view is split into subviews that progressively reveal more information. Applying the mutual-information chain rule produces unconditional and conditional terms, each responsible for a smaller part of the total. The authors also formulate an efficiently approximated contrastive lower bound for the conditional terms.

In a synthetic setting, DEMI captures more mutual information than standard contrastive bounds without decomposition. Experiments also show better learned representations in a vision domain and for dialogue generation. These findings support estimating shared information in manageable portions: the decomposition preserves the overall information objective while making its individual components more suitable for contrastive approximation.
icml-2021-decomposed-mutual-information-.tldr: DEMI divides mutual-information estimation into smaller contrastive problems to reduce underestimation and improve learned representations.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning must learn both how to interpret images and how to act. This paper separates those jobs so that learning visual features does not depend entirely on reward-driven policy training. Its unsupervised task, Augmented Temporal Contrast, trains a convolutional encoder to associate observations occurring a short time apart while applying image augmentations and a contrastive loss.

In online experiments, using only this task to train the encoder matches or exceeds end-to-end reinforcement learning in most tested environments. The authors also pretrain encoders on expert demonstrations and freeze their weights during subsequent policy learning. In that comparison, agents using ATC encoders outperform agents using the other evaluated unsupervised-learning methods.

Further experiments train shared encoders across environments and demonstrate generalization to different downstream tasks. The work also examines ATC components and introduces an augmentation that supports replaying compressed latent images when reinforcement learning needs augmentation. Results across DeepMind Control, DeepMind Lab, and Atari support the practical value of learning reusable visual features separately from the policy.
icml-2021-decoupling-representation-lear.tldr: Augmented Temporal Contrast learns visual features independently of rewards and supports strong reinforcement-learning performance across varied benchmarks.

paragraphs: In fully cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents work toward a shared outcome while each sees only part of the environment. Their policies also change during learning, adding uncertainty to the outcomes each agent experiences. This paper addresses that uncertainty by combining distributional reinforcement learning with methods that factor a team value function into individual utilities.

The Distributional Value Function Factorization framework, or DFAC, extends individual utilities from single deterministic values to random variables. It represents the quantile function of the team’s total return through a mixture of quantiles. This provides a way to extend factorization methods based on expected returns so that they can model distributions of returns.

The authors demonstrate the framework on a two-step matrix game with stochastic rewards and evaluate it on every Super Hard task in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge. They report better performance than expected-value factorization baselines. The results support the usefulness of incorporating return distributions into cooperative value factorization when agents face uncertain outcomes and incomplete observations.
icml-2021-dfac-framework-factorizing-the.tldr: DFAC extends cooperative multi-agent value factorization to return distributions using a quantile mixture.

paragraphs: A graph embedding represents nodes as points in a space, and the geometry of that space shapes which relationships are easy to express. Directed graphs add a particular challenge because a connection from one node to another has an orientation. This paper investigates embedding spaces and a likelihood model designed to incorporate that directional structure.

The proposed model combines a pseudo-Riemannian metric, nontrivial global topology, and a likelihood function with an explicit preferred direction. These components jointly determine how the embedding represents relationships. The approach therefore treats the choice of geometry and the way links are modeled as coordinated parts of the representation.

The authors evaluate link prediction on synthetic graphs and real directed graphs from language applications and biology. They show that low-dimensional cylindrical Minkowski and anti-de Sitter spaces can match or improve on representations using higher-dimensional curved Riemannian spaces. The finding suggests that choosing a geometry suited to directionality can be more effective than simply increasing the number of embedding dimensions.
icml-2021-directed-graph-embeddings-in-p.tldr: Direction-aware pseudo-Riemannian embeddings can represent directed graphs as well as or better than higher-dimensional Riemannian alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decisions in which using an option reduces its immediate value, while leaving it idle allows its expected reward to recover. At each time step, the decision maker may choose at most K of N options. Recovery is nonparametric, allowing the problem to describe reward patterns without prescribing a particular recovery formula.

The authors construct purely periodic policies for maximizing cumulative expected reward. When the model is known, their policy achieves an approximation ratio of order 1 minus a term proportional to 1 divided by the square root of K. This guarantee approaches optimality as the number of options that can be selected per period grows.

When the model must also be learned, an upper-confidence-bound policy has approximately N times the square root of the time horizon in regret against the offline benchmark, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The framework connects scheduling and learning: actions must balance current reward against future recovery. The authors suggest that this design may also adapt to other problems with recovering, nonstationary rewards.
icml-2021-dynamic-planning-and-learning-.tldr: Periodic scheduling and confidence-based learning provide guarantees for bandits whose rewards recover while options remain unused.

paragraphs: Kernel approximation can reduce the cost of machine-learning methods that rely on kernel functions. Polynomial kernels are especially useful because Taylor expansions can connect them to other kernels. This paper targets the computational cost that arises when an accurate approximation requires a polynomial of high degree.

Earlier oblivious-sketching techniques reduced dependence on the degree from exponential to polynomial. That improvement is useful for Gaussian-kernel approximation, where the required degree can be polylogarithmic. For more slowly growing kernels, including neural tangent and arc cosine kernels, the degree needs to be polynomial, so the remaining dependence still creates a substantial slowdown.

The authors introduce an oblivious sketch that removes degree dependence from the leading runtime term. They combine it with a new sampling scheme and report the fastest approximation algorithms for a broad family of slowly growing kernels. The result concerns the dominant computational cost; it does not claim that every runtime term becomes independent of degree. Its significance is making high-degree polynomial approximation more computationally practical.
icml-2021-fast-sketching-of-polynomial-k.tldr: A new oblivious sketch removes polynomial-degree dependence from the leading runtime term for approximating a broad family of kernels.

paragraphs: Explaining a graphical model can involve more than assigning importance to individual nodes. A change introduced at a source can propagate through the graph, and an attribution method can try to quantify that propagation. This paper develops recursive Shapley value, or RSV, as a model-agnostic approach to this flow-based explanation problem.

RSV generalizes several existing node-based attribution methods while satisfying a set of axioms formulated for flows. The authors establish that RSV is the unique method satisfying that particular set of axioms. This gives the method a precise mathematical justification: its attribution rule follows from specified requirements about how effects should be assigned through the graph.

The method also has a natural characterization for linear models and supports mediation analysis in nonlinear models, connecting attribution to the role of intermediate parts of a graph. It satisfies implementation invariance, sensitivity, monotonicity, and affine scale invariance. Together, these results position RSV as a unified way to reason about propagated contributions while retaining several established desirable properties of explanations.
icml-2021-flow-based-attribution-in-grap.tldr: Recursive Shapley value attributes how source changes propagate through graphical models and uniquely satisfies a specified set of flow axioms.

paragraphs: Permuting neurons can produce different parameter settings with the same network behavior. This paper studies how those symmetries shape critical points and global minima when networks gain extra neurons. Its starting assumption is a network of minimal layer widths whose zero-loss minima are isolated points related by permutations.

Under that assumption, adding one neuron to each layer is sufficient to connect all those minima into a single manifold. For a two-layer network with h extra neurons, the authors describe connected affine subspaces forming the global-minimum manifold, each having dimension at least h. They also count affine subspaces of symmetry-induced critical points associated with narrower networks.

Closed-form combinatorial formulas reveal a change as width increases. With mild overparameterization, symmetry-induced critical subspaces outnumber the subspaces forming the global minima; with much greater overparameterization, the ordering reverses. These results explain how additional width reorganizes the loss landscape. They provide geometric insight into optimization without asserting that a particular training algorithm necessarily reaches a global minimum.
icml-2021-geometry-of-the-loss-landscape.tldr: Under stated assumptions, extra neurons connect permutation-related minima and change the balance of symmetry-induced critical and minimum subspaces.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search often evaluates many candidate networks by letting them share weights within a supernet. In one-shot sharing, an operation uses the same weights across every architecture containing it. This paper argues that the resulting inability to tailor weights to different paths reduces the reliability of candidate evaluations.

K-shot NAS introduces multiple supernets whose operation weights form a dictionary. Each architecture receives weights constructed as a convex combination of dictionary entries, with a simplex-net producing its architecture-specific combination. When K exceeds one, this supports a higher-rank approximation to the matrix of independently trained weights. Sharing becomes adaptable to each candidate path.

The supernets and simplex-net can be trained iteratively, and the method also extends architecture search to channel choices. Benchmark experiments report significant improvements in the accuracy of path evaluation and in resulting performance. The main contribution is a more flexible sharing mechanism: it retains shared training while giving different architectures access to different combinations of learned operation weights.
icml-2021-k-shot-nas-learnable-weight-sh.tldr: K-shot NAS learns architecture-specific mixtures of shared weights to improve the reliability of neural architecture evaluation.

paragraphs: When hypotheses arise from selecting features in data, statistical inference must account for that selection. Conditional selective inference does this by conditioning on the event that produced the chosen features. The paper focuses on stepwise feature selection, where this event can be described using linear or quadratic inequalities.

Existing approaches often condition on extra information to keep the calculations manageable. That over-conditioning reduces statistical power, weakening the ability to detect effects. The authors introduce a homotopy-based method that overcomes this limitation and supports more general selection procedures. Its purpose is to make the required conditional analysis tractable without the same loss of power.

As a concrete example, the paper develops inference for forward-backward stepwise selection with an AIC-based stopping rule. The authors show that their approach is not adversely affected by this procedure’s increased complexity, and experiments demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution links computational technique to statistical usefulness: handling a richer selection process need not impose the same power penalty associated with earlier tractability choices.
icml-2021-more-powerful-and-general-sele.tldr: A homotopy-based selective-inference method reduces power loss from over-conditioning and handles more complex stepwise feature selection.

paragraphs: Repeated neural-network training runs can produce different results, making small performance improvements difficult to distinguish from ordinary variability. Training many copies can help assess that uncertainty, but it adds time and cost. This paper establishes an experimental protocol for separating the effects of different sources of nondeterminism on the diversity of trained models.

Across the sources examined, the authors find surprisingly similar effects on measures of model diversity. They explain this through instability of the full training procedure: a very small initial difference can lead to a substantially different final outcome. Their demonstration shows that changing just one bit in initial parameters can produce models that converge to widely different values.

The paper then proposes two approaches for reducing how this instability affects variation between runs. Its central contribution is to connect observed model diversity to the sensitivity of training as a whole. This helps explain why different sources of nondeterminism can have comparable effects, and why evaluating small claimed gains requires attention to the variability generated during optimization.
icml-2021-nondeterminism-and-instability.tldr: Experiments identify training instability as a key reason different sources of nondeterminism produce similar variation across neural-network runs.

paragraphs: Attention-based sequence models can use distant history, but preserving and attending to many past states is computationally expensive. This paper starts from the observation that past information differs in importance. Expire-Span learns what to retain and what to let expire, allowing memory use to depend on the relevance of its contents.

By discarding information judged irrelevant, the method enables Transformers to attend across tens of thousands of previous time steps without preserving every state. The authors test whether models can identify and keep critical information on reinforcement-learning tasks designed to challenge that ability. They report strong performance, supporting the usefulness of learned forgetting for selective long-term memory.

The paper also reports state-of-the-art results on very long-context tasks, including character-level language modeling and a task involving moving objects presented frame by frame. Efficiency comparisons show faster training and lower memory use than existing approaches. These findings connect selective retention to both task performance and computational savings: a long usable history need not require keeping all previous representations.
icml-2021-not-all-memories-are-created-e.tldr: Expire-Span learns which memories to retain, enabling efficient attention over long histories with strong reported task performance.

paragraphs: This paper develops a central-path algorithm for linear programming that uses sketching to reduce computational work. Its overall running time matches the state-of-the-art results discussed in the abstract. The distinguishing contribution is a combination of properties that those earlier methods did not provide together.

The algorithm works inside the central-path iterations through an iterate-and-sketch approach, supported by a new coordinate-wise embedding technique. It is both oblivious and feasible: its sketching approach is not tailored to the input in the way a non-oblivious method is, while retaining feasibility. The comparison in the paper contrasts this combination with earlier feasible but non-oblivious and oblivious but infeasible approaches.

The method can also use sparse sketching matrices, speeding up online matrix-vector multiplication compared with the dense sketching matrices required by the cited oblivious approach. Beyond linear programming, the framework generalizes to a wider class of convex problems, including empirical risk minimization. Its significance is combining a competitive runtime guarantee with feasibility and a computationally useful choice of sparse sketches.
icml-2021-oblivious-sketching-based-cent.tldr: A sketching-based central-path method matches leading linear-programming runtimes while combining obliviousness, feasibility, and support for sparse sketches.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning has the potential to learn efficiently from limited interactions, but successful exploration remains a difficulty for existing empirical methods. PC-MLP addresses that gap with policy-cover-guided exploration. The paper studies an algorithm intended to be efficient both in computation and in the number of samples needed for learning.

The theoretical results cover two model classes: Kernelized Nonlinear Regulators and linear Markov decision processes. For each, the algorithm guarantees polynomial sample complexity and requires access only to a planning oracle. This makes the planning-oracle interface an explicit part of the result, while the sample-efficiency guarantee applies to the specified model classes.

Experiments first test control tasks where exploration is challenging and existing empirical model-based approaches fail completely. The proposed method succeeds in demonstrating flexibility and effectiveness there. It also retains excellent performance on common dense-reward control benchmarks that require less exploration. Together, these findings show that addressing exploration can improve difficult tasks while preserving strong results in the more routinely rewarded settings examined.
icml-2021-pc-mlp-model-based-reinforceme.tldr: PC-MLP improves model-based exploration and provides polynomial sample-complexity guarantees for two model classes using a planning oracle.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples make small input changes that alter a classifier’s decision. Many attacks assume that querying the same input gives a deterministic answer, so randomized outputs can disrupt their operation. This paper introduces PopSkipJump, a decision-based attack designed to handle classifiers whose responses are probabilistic.

The method builds on HopSkipJump, an attack developed for deterministic classifiers. PopSkipJump adjusts how many queries it uses to preserve the original attack’s output quality across different noise levels. As noise decreases, its query efficiency approaches that of HopSkipJump. The adaptation therefore connects the amount of information gathered from the classifier to the uncertainty in its responses.

The authors evaluate several noise models, including existing randomized defenses, and find that the tested defenses provide almost no additional robustness against decision-based attacks. The result distinguishes disrupting a deterministic attack from resisting an attack adapted to randomness. In the examined settings, probabilistic responses call for an adjusted query strategy but do little to prevent adversarial examples from being found.
icml-2021-popskipjump-decision-based-att.tldr: PopSkipJump adapts decision-based attacks to randomized classifier outputs and finds little added robustness from the tested randomized defenses.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards leave reinforcement-learning agents with little guidance, making redundant actions especially costly. This paper proposes the k-Shortest-Path constraint on trajectories to suppress unnecessary behavior, such as repeatedly moving back and forth. The authors show that any optimal policy satisfies this constraint in the setting they study.

Applying the constraint as a strict exclusion rule would prevent exploration of state-action pairs on violating trajectories. However, that exclusion can interfere with the convergence of reinforcement-learning algorithms. The proposed practical approach instead introduces a cost that penalizes violations, allowing the constraint to guide learning without completely removing those possibilities.

A tabular experiment shows that the constraint can substantially reduce the trajectory space. Experiments on MiniGrid, DeepMind Lab, Atari, and Fetch report significant improvements to proximal policy optimization and better results than existing novelty-seeking methods, including count-based exploration. The findings extend to continuous control in the tested tasks. They support improving sample efficiency by reducing redundant exploration and exploitation, alongside the more familiar goal of seeking new experiences.
icml-2021-shortest-path-constrained-rein.tldr: Penalizing violations of a shortest-path constraint reduces redundant actions and improves sample efficiency in tested sparse-reward tasks.

paragraphs: Lipschitz-constrained convolutional networks are useful for provable adversarial robustness and stable training, but preserving gradient norms is important to avoid vanishing gradients. Existing gradient-norm-preserving convolutions can train slowly, reduce accuracy, and lack guarantees for their approximations. This paper introduces Skew Orthogonal Convolution, or SOC, to address these issues.

SOC uses the mathematical fact that exponentiating a skew-symmetric matrix produces an orthogonal matrix. The authors first construct a convolution filter with a skew-symmetric Jacobian, then express its exponential through a Taylor series. The ideal construction is orthogonal; the efficient implementation retains finitely many terms and comes with a proven bound on the resulting approximation error.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show that SOC trains large, provably Lipschitz convolutional networks significantly faster than previous approaches. The authors also report significant gains in standard accuracy and certified robust accuracy. The contribution combines a norm-preserving mathematical construction with controlled approximation, linking the desired structural guarantee to an implementation that improves the measured training and prediction outcomes.
icml-2021-skew-orthogonal-convolutions-7.tldr: SOC uses skew-symmetric matrix exponentials and bounded approximations to train Lipschitz convolutional networks faster with improved reported accuracy.

paragraphs: Representing a scene as objects can help an agent reason and plan, but partial visibility creates uncertainty about what those objects are doing. A single scene representation may not capture that uncertainty. Structured World Belief learns object-centric belief states that maintain multiple possible explanations of the scene.

The method uses Sequential Monte Carlo to infer these hypotheses and combines it with an object-centric dynamics model designed around object permanence. This enables it to track object states even during long periods of invisibility. It also allows attention to move flexibly to any image location, helping object tracking in circumstances where previous models restricted that flexibility.

Experiments show more accurate and robust filtering and generation with the object-centric beliefs. The authors also demonstrate improvements in reinforcement learning, planning, and supervised reasoning. The findings connect structured uncertainty to downstream usefulness: maintaining several plausible object states can improve both the model’s account of a partially observed world and the tasks that depend on that account.
icml-2021-structured-world-belief-for-re.tldr: Structured World Belief tracks multiple object-centric scene hypotheses to improve inference and decision-making under partial observability.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives, including support vector machines and least absolute deviation, involve structured sums of nonsmooth convex terms. This paper introduces a primal-dual optimization algorithm that combines variance reduction with accelerated dual averaging. Its analysis shows how exploiting that structure improves the computational cost of reaching a desired accuracy.

For n samples, primal dimension d, and target accuracy epsilon, the general convex bound is O(nd log min{1/epsilon, n} + d/epsilon). With strong convexity, the final term becomes d divided by the square root of epsilon. Compared with the stated previous bounds, both results remove a square-root-of-n factor from the accuracy-dependent term. The stronger setting also provides guarantees on distance to the optimal solution.

These complexities improve on lower bounds for general finite-sum convex optimization because the algorithm uses additional structure; the results therefore concern a more specific problem class. Numerical experiments show competitive performance against existing approaches. The contribution combines sharper theoretical scaling with an algorithm and analysis described as simpler and more direct.
icml-2021-variance-reduction-via-primal-.tldr: A structured primal-dual algorithm removes a square-root sample-count factor from key complexity terms in nonsmooth convex finite-sum optimization.

paragraphs: Object detectors often produce redundant predictions that are removed by non-maximum suppression, a nondifferentiable step. This paper investigates how detectors can instead learn to produce one prediction per object. It identifies one-to-one positive-sample assignment during training as a key factor, while also finding that this assignment alone leaves redundancy in previous detectors.

The missing ingredient is classification cost in the matching rule used to assign positive samples. Earlier detectors considered only location cost. Adding classification cost makes the examined detectors produce one-to-one predictions at inference. The paper uses a score-gap concept to explain how matching choices influence the separation between prediction scores.

Classification-aware matching favors the highest-scoring positive samples during training and reduces noisy positives introduced by location-only matching. This enlarges the score gap and helps explain the resulting reduction in duplicate predictions. The authors also demonstrate advantages in crowded scenes. The work clarifies that end-to-end detection depends on how training matches predictions to objects, including both the number of positive assignments and the information used to choose them.
icml-2021-what-makes-for-end-to-end-obje.tldr: One-to-one assignment combined with classification-aware matching enables the examined detectors to avoid redundant predictions without non-maximum suppression.
